sections.title: Underwriting Performance
sections.subtitle: GAAP combined ratio and its components, by segment

charts.title: Combined Ratio by Segment
charts.annotation: 100% is break-even; below 100% means the segment earned an underwriting profit before investment income.

charts.title: Loss, Expense & Catastrophe Ratio
charts.annotation: Loss ratio + expense ratio = combined ratio. Catastrophe loss ratio is the part of the loss ratio from storms/wildfire, shown separately because it swings most.

charts.title: Net Earned Premium & Underwriting Income
charts.annotation: Underwriting income is earned premium less losses and expenses, before investment income -- the core profitability test of the P&C business on its own, independent of the equity portfolio.

charts.title: Book Value per Share & Value Creation Ratio
charts.annotation: Value creation ratio = BVPS growth + dividend yield, management's own scorecard metric; quarterly points are trailing contributions within the fiscal year, not annualised.

combinedRatio.title: Combined ratio by segment
combinedRatio.content:
The combined ratio is losses and loss-adjustment expenses plus underwriting expenses, divided by earned premium. Below 100% means the segment made an underwriting profit before investment income; above 100% means premiums alone did not cover claims and expenses.

For Cincinnati Financial: commercial lines is the largest book (~53% of premium) and sets the overall ratio; excess & surplus and Cincinnati Re/Global are the newer, fastest-growing lines and have been running a lower (better) ratio than commercial and personal lines. Personal lines carries concentrated California wildfire exposure and is the most volatile of the three.

What to watch:

  • Personal lines spiking on catastrophe quarters (wildfire, hail, hurricane)
  • Whether E&S/Cincinnati Re keep outgrowing and outperforming the legacy commercial book
  • Sustained quarters above 100% in any segment -- rate increases take several quarters to earn through

lossExpenseRatio.title: Loss, expense & catastrophe ratio
lossExpenseRatio.content:
The loss ratio (claims paid and reserved, over earned premium) and expense ratio (underwriting expenses over earned premium) are the two components that sum to the combined ratio. The catastrophe loss ratio is the slice of the loss ratio attributable to named storms, wildfire and other catastrophe events.

For Cincinnati Financial: the expense ratio is normally the steadier of the two (agency commissions, overhead); the loss ratio is where catastrophe losses and reserve releases/strengthening show up, so a loss-ratio spike with a flat expense ratio is almost always a cat quarter, not a pricing problem.

What to watch:

  • Catastrophe loss ratio relative to the broader loss ratio -- how much of any quarter's deterioration is weather versus attritional losses
  • Expense ratio drifting up, which signals agency commission or overhead growth outpacing premium

nwpSegment.title: Net written premium by segment
nwpSegment.content:
Net written premium (NWP) is new and renewal premium booked in the period, net of reinsurance ceded -- the forward-looking volume metric, ahead of earned premium which recognises revenue ratably over the policy term.

For Cincinnati Financial: commercial lines dominates NWP, but excess & surplus and Cincinnati Re/Global have been growing NWP at roughly double-digit rates (management cited ~5-7% E&S and +11-13% reinsurance growth through 9M 2026) while personal lines growth reflects deliberate repricing of the wildfire-exposed California book rather than volume chasing.

What to watch:

  • Segment mix shift toward E&S/reinsurance, which the company frames as its most profitable growth
  • Personal lines NWP growth driven by rate versus policy count

underwritingIncome.title: Net earned premium & underwriting income
underwritingIncome.content:
Net earned premium is premium recognised as revenue over the policy period; underwriting income is earned premium less losses, loss-adjustment expenses and underwriting expenses -- profit (or loss) from the insurance business alone, before any investment income or realized/unrealized gains.

For Cincinnati Financial: because roughly 40% of invested assets sit in publicly traded equities, reported net income swings with the stock market independently of underwriting -- this chart isolates the part of earnings that is actually insurance performance.

What to watch:

  • Underwriting income turning negative in catastrophe-heavy quarters (it did in Q2 2026)
  • Underwriting income as a share of earned premium, trending versus the combined ratio chart above

bookValue.title: Book value per share & value creation ratio
bookValue.content:
Book value per share (BVPS) is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding. The value creation ratio is management's own scorecard metric: BVPS growth plus dividend yield, a total-return proxy independent of the share price.

For Cincinnati Financial: BVPS is unusually sensitive to equity-market moves given the large common-stock portfolio, so a quarter's BVPS change mixes underwriting results, bond mark-to-market and stock-market performance -- it is not a pure measure of operating progress the way it is for a typical industrial.

What to watch:

  • BVPS declines driven by equity-market drawdowns versus by underwriting losses
  • Value creation ratio against the company's long-stated double-digit annual target

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Cincinnati Financial Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
